name: COPA
summary: 500 hand-written questions on everyday cause and effect, each asking which of two alternatives is the more plausible cause or result of a short premise.
overview:
COPA, the Choice of Plausible Alternatives, tests commonsense causal reasoning in its barest form. Each question gives a one-sentence premise and two alternatives and asks which alternative is the more plausible cause of the premise, or the more plausible result of it. Melissa Roemmele, Cosmin Adrian Bejan, and Andrew Gordon released it in 2011, at a time when open-domain commonsense reasoning had no shared evaluation to measure progress against. It holds 1,000 questions, split evenly into a development set and a test set. [Paper](https://web.archive.org/web/20210513111412/http://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/publications/AAAI-SPRING11A.PDF)

The authors wrote every question themselves, and the way they wrote the wrong answers is what makes the task hard. To spread the questions across everyday life, they drew topics from two sources: randomly chosen personal stories from a corpus of a million weblog posts written in August and September 2008, and randomly chosen subject terms from the Library of Congress Thesaurus for Graphic Materials. The blogs supplied mostly social and mental topics, and the thesaurus mostly physical ones. For each topic they wrote a premise and a correct alternative linked by a causal relation. They then wrote a wrong alternative that matches the correct one in form and fits the same scene but has no direct causal link. In the paper's example, "The man fell unconscious" has the cause "The assailant struck the man in the head" and the decoy "The assailant took the man's wallet", both of which come from the same assault scene. The goal was that associating words with a scene would not be enough to choose. [Paper](https://web.archive.org/web/20210513111412/http://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/publications/AAAI-SPRING11A.PDF)

Scores on the test set have moved from near chance to near the ceiling. The authors' best word-association baseline reached 58.8%, the winning system of the SemEval-2012 shared task built on COPA reached 63.4%, and OpenAI's first GPT reported 78.6%. In 2019 COPA became one of the ten tasks of the SuperGLUE benchmark, where BERT scored 70.6% and the estimated human score was 100%. By January 2021 an ensemble of DeBERTa models scored 98.4% on SuperGLUE's evaluation server. [Results list](https://web.archive.org/web/20240402061922/https://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/copa.html), [SuperGLUE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00537), and [DeBERTa paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.03654)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete COPA test set: all 500 questions of `copa-test.xml`, numbered 501 to 1000, with the answers from the package's `gold.test` file. The 500-question development set is not imported, and neither are the baseline answer files or the significance-test program that the package also ships. The publisher's address no longer serves the project page or the package. The snapshot is read from the Internet Archive's unmodified capture of the package, which is pinned by its SHA-256 digest because the package has no version history. Its readme says "Version 1. March 2011" and its files are dated 2011-03-04. SuperGLUE distributes COPA as 400 training, 100 validation, and 500 test questions and scores test answers on its own server; this snapshot follows the original release. [Archived project page](https://web.archive.org/web/20240402061922/https://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/copa.html) and [SuperGLUE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00537)

Each Task Prompt gives the premise, then the question that the publisher's readable development-set file uses for that direction: "What was the CAUSE of this?" for the 250 cause questions and "What happened as a RESULT?" for the 250 effect questions. The two alternatives follow, labelled the way the project page labels its examples. The sentences are reproduced exactly as published, including a leading space that two alternatives carry upstream. They are short by design, written in the past tense and without names or slang: premises average 6.1 words and alternatives 5.0.

The Solution is the correct alternative, given with its number. The position of the correct alternative was randomized and is exactly balanced: 250 questions have alternative 1 as the answer and 250 have alternative 2. Keys are the upstream question numbers. The importer uses only Python's standard library. It checks the digest of the package, that the test file holds questions 501 to 1000 once each with a premise and two alternatives, that the cause and effect questions and the answer positions are each split 250 to 250, and that the answer recorded in the question file matches the separate answer file for every question. It can be rerun with python3 data/copa/import.py.
scoring:
COPA is scored as accuracy: the fraction of the 500 test questions for which a system picks the correct alternative. Because the answer position is balanced, random guessing scores exactly 50%. The package includes a significance test based on approximate randomization, which compares two systems' answer files, and the authors ask that results be reported on both the development and test sets. Outside SuperGLUE there is no submission server, and the answers ship with the questions, so published scores on this test set are self-reported. [Paper](https://web.archive.org/web/20210513111412/http://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/publications/AAAI-SPRING11A.PDF) and [archived project page](https://web.archive.org/web/20240402061922/https://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/copa.html)

Humans find the task easy. To validate the questions, ten native English-speaking volunteers outside the project each answered 200, so that every question had two raters, and their agreement was a Cohen's kappa of 0.965. The authors replaced the 26 questions that a rater answered differently from the author's intent and validated the replacements with two more raters, so every question in the final set was answered as intended by both of its raters. SuperGLUE likewise estimates human accuracy on COPA at 100%. [Paper](https://web.archive.org/web/20210513111412/http://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/publications/AAAI-SPRING11A.PDF) and [SuperGLUE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00537)

Benchopedia stores the questions and their answers. It does not run a scorer or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
The alternatives carry cues that work without the premise. Kavumba and colleagues found single words whose presence in an alternative predicts the answer more often than chance. The word `a`, for instance, occurs in one alternative but not the other in 21.2% of the questions they counted, and in those questions it marks the correct alternative 57.5% of the time. A RoBERTa model shown only the two alternatives, with the premise hidden, averaged 59.6%. They split the test set into the 190 questions such a model solves in every run and the 310 it does not. Fine-tuned BERT-large scored 83.9% on the first group and 71.9% on the second, and fine-tuned RoBERTa-large 91.6% and 85.3%. They released Balanced COPA, a version built to remove these single-word cues. [Balanced COPA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00225)

The test set is small and stylized. With 500 questions, each question is worth 0.2 percentage points, so close results need the significance test the authors provide. The questions were written by the authors in one deliberately plain style, with short past-tense sentences, no names, and a narrow set of question forms. Accuracy on them may not carry over to causal reasoning in ordinary text. [Paper](https://web.archive.org/web/20210513111412/http://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/publications/AAAI-SPRING11A.PDF)

The answers have been public with the questions since 2011, and COPA is part of SuperGLUE and the source of several translated versions, so a model may have seen these questions and their answers in training. The authors ask researchers not to study the 500 test questions and to evaluate on them only once, after all tuning on the development set is done. Publishing the questions here does not change that request, but a reported score is only as clean as the practice behind it. COPA carries no canary string. [Archived project page](https://web.archive.org/web/20240402061922/https://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/copa.html)
